blogs.title: From Right-to-Control to Fraudulent Inducement: The Fifth Circuit’s Property Analysis in Constantinescu
blogs.description: This post unpacks how the Fifth Circuit threads the needle between Ciminelli’s rejection of the right-to-control theory and Kousisis’s embrace of fraudulent inducement, and applies that synthesis to 18 U.S.C. § 1348. It explains why inducing followers to buy stocks with lies is a scheme to obtain money—not merely to withhold economic information—and what that means for future charging decisions under § 1348 vs. mail/wire fraud and Rule 10b-5. It also highlights open questions about the limits of ‘property’ in influencer-driven markets and the potential for broader DOJ reliance on § 1348 in market-touting cases.

blogs.title: Intent Without Loss? Mens Rea Under § 1348 After Kousisis and the Fifth Circuit’s Take
blogs.description: Focusing on the opinion’s intent-to-defraud analysis, this piece explores the court’s conclusion that a profit motive can satisfy the required intent even if victims receive market-value securities and suffer no net economic loss. It discusses how the panel reads Kousisis to decouple fraud from bottom-line harm, why “having money in mind” matters, and what that portends for defense strategies, jury instructions, and the line between self-enrichment and victim harm in criminal securities fraud.

blogs.title: What an Indictment Must Say: Pleading Standards for Criminal Securities Fraud in the Fifth Circuit
blogs.description: This post examines the procedural backbone of the decision: de novo review of indictment sufficiency and the requirement to accept allegations as true. It analyzes how the Constantinescu indictment cleared the bar—enumerating § 1348’s elements, describing the pump-and-dump mechanics, and alleging material misstatements and profits—and offers practice takeaways for prosecutors and defense counsel. It also flags issues the court leaves for later stages (materiality proofs, causation theories, and any First Amendment arguments about market-touting speech).

blogs.title: Influencers, Pump-and-Dumps, and the Next Wave of ‘FinTok’ Prosecutions
blogs.description: Zooming out to enforcement implications, this post considers how Constantinescu positions DOJ to pursue social-media touting schemes as fraudulent inducement under § 1348. It distinguishes nonactionable puffery from concrete lies about trading positions and exit plans, notes the historical ‘scalping’ concerns in market promotion, and previews practical compliance takeaways for online personalities, Discord/Telegram communities, and emerging-asset promoters. It also assesses spillover effects beyond equities, where prosecutors might toggle between § 1348 and traditional wire-fraud theories.
